entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Tommaso Rodari (c. 1460–1525) was a prominent Swiss-Italian sculptor and architect, primarily active in the Ticino region and Lombardy during the late Quattrocento and early Cinquecento. His artistic output, characterized by a distinctive fusion of Lombard Renaissance classicism and lingering Gothic influences, played a pivotal role in shaping the architectural and sculptural identity of key ecclesiastical structures in Northern Italy and Southern Switzerland. A significant figure from the Rodari family of artists originating from Maroggia, his career exemplifies the regional artistic developments on the cusp of the High Renaissance.

Rodari's most enduring and significant achievement is the extensive sculptural decoration of the façade of Como Cathedral (Duomo di Como), where he was actively engaged from 1487 until his death in 1525. He is specifically credited with the intricate portal sculptures, including the iconic, classically-inspired figures of Pliny the Elder and Pliny the Younger, which uniquely integrate classical humanism with the Christian iconography of a major cathedral. Beyond Como, Rodari contributed to other notable projects, designing and overseeing construction for the Sanctuary of the Madonna del Sasso near Locarno (c. 1480–1500) and contributing sculptural elements to the Church of Santa Maria degli Angeli in Lugano, further disseminating his rich, detailed ornamental style.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Tommaso Rodari's extensive sculptural program for Como Cathedral, particularly the integration of classical figures like the Plinys, established a unique regional artistic synthesis. His work influenced generations of local sculptors and architects, leaving a lasting stylistic mark on the Lombard-Ticinese region.
